title: Why Almost Nobody Lives on Florida's Big Bend Coast
sources: Landsat imagery courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey

paragraphs.text: On the night Hurricane Helene came ashore in September 2024, a tide gauge at Cedar Key, Florida, measured the sea nine point three feet above the normal high-tide line. That gauge had been reporting since 1914. In all those years, it had never recorded water that high. And Cedar Key is not a city. It is a town of seven hundred and thirty-six people, on a stretch of coast where a town that size counts as a big one.

paragraphs.text: Florida is home to about twenty-three point four million people, and long stretches of its coast are lined with cities and beach towns. Pinellas County alone, around St. Petersburg, holds almost a million. But follow the same Gulf coast north, to the long curve where the peninsula turns into the Panhandle. This is the Big Bend. Four counties along that shore, Jefferson, Taylor, Dixie and Levy, hold about a hundred and three thousand people between them. Seen from space at night, this stretch of coast is almost dark.

paragraphs.text: The towns along it are tiny. Horseshoe Beach has a hundred and seventy-three people. St. Marks, three hundred and twelve. Yankeetown, six hundred and thirty-three. The biggest town behind this coast, Perry, has about seven thousand three hundred, and it sits well inland. There is no big city, no resort strip, and for most of its length, no beach at all.

paragraphs.text: Over the next few minutes you'll see a seafloor so flat that three miles out from Cedar Key the water is barely deeper than a person is tall. A town that once hoped to be Florida's great Gulf port and lost it to a railroad built somewhere else. A canal across Florida that was stopped at twenty-eight percent. And why that same flat seafloor sent the water at Cedar Key higher than anyone had ever measured. So why does a state that lives on its coastline leave this one almost empty? It isn't one thing. It's five, and they all start in the same place. The first reason is under the water.

chapters.title: A Sea That Forgot to Get Deep

paragraphs.text: Stand on almost any beach in Florida and walk into the sea, and the bottom drops away. Off Pensacola Beach, we measured the distance to the point where the water is ten metres deep, about thirty-three feet, using NOAA's global seafloor model. It's about a mile. Off Miami Beach, about a mile and a quarter. Off Panama City Beach, less than a third of a mile.

stat.label: = 33 ft: the line we measured to
stat.source: Own measurement: NOAA ETOPO 2022 seafloor model (60 arc-sec)

paragraphs.text: Now do the same along the Big Bend. Off Keaton Beach, the ten-metre line is about thirteen miles out. Off Steinhatchee and St. Marks, about sixteen. Off Cedar Key, about fifteen. Off Crystal River, at the southern end, about twenty-two miles. Even Clearwater and Naples, on the same Gulf, get there in about seven and a half.

paragraphs.text: Go three miles out from shore and the difference is even easier to picture. Off Cedar Key, our measurement puts the water at about five and a half feet deep. Off Keaton Beach, about eight. Off Pensacola, about seventy feet. Off Miami, about two hundred and seventy. And at thirty miles out from Cedar Key, the Gulf is still only about fifty feet deep. Thirty miles out from Pensacola, it is already more than three hundred. These numbers come from a model with cells about a mile across, so treat them as rough, but the pattern is not subtle.

paragraphs.text: Geologists at the U.S. Geological Survey put a number on how gentle this slope is: about one in five thousand. That works out to roughly one foot of depth for every mile you travel out to sea. It is so flat, their report notes, that this coast has been described as an "incipient epicontinental sea": a place where the ocean is only just beginning to spread over the land.

stat.label: Slope of the Big Bend's marsh coast
Depth gained heading out to sea

document.text: such a low gradient (1:5,000) that it has been referred to as an incipient epicontinental sea
document.title: USGS, Big Bend coast

shots.on_screen_text: Where the land runs into the Gulf, Cedar Key

paragraphs.text: That flat floor explains the first strange thing about the Big Bend. It has almost no beaches. The same USGS work describes the marsh coast here as lower in wave energy than the sandy coast to the south, and the region as sediment-starved. The Gulf in front of it is small and sheltered, its waves are weak, and little sand ever reaches this shore. So instead of a beach, the land simply runs out into salt marsh, and the marsh runs out into the sea.

stat.label: Marsh, not sand, for most of the Big Bend

shots.on_screen_text: Sandy coast to the south: Clearwater Beach

document.text: Big Bend region ... is considered sediment-starved

paragraphs.text: And the shallow water isn't empty. It is carpeted with seagrass. The Big Bend Seagrasses Aquatic Preserve covers nine hundred and eighty-four thousand acres, the largest aquatic preserve in Florida, and one of the largest continuous seagrass meadows in the Gulf. Which raises a question we'll come back to at the end: is this coast a failure to develop, or one of the few places Florida never got around to ruining? Tell me in the comments which way you lean.

ask.text: A failure to develop, or a coast Florida never ruined?

paragraphs.text: For people who wanted to build here, though, that seafloor was a problem with no answer. A port needs deep water close to shore. Ships can't sail to a dock across fifteen miles of water you could almost wade. And there was a second problem, one you can't see from the sea at all, because it's underneath the land.

shots.on_screen_text: Shallows off Keaton Beach and Steinhatchee

shots.photo: File:St Marks NWR Rx Fire in salt water marsh (7439799476).jpg

paragraphs.text: Most of the land behind this coast sits on limestone, covered by a thin layer of sand. Rainwater soaks straight through the sand and slowly dissolves the rock underneath. Over thousands of years, that has turned the ground into something closer to a sponge: caves, sinkholes and underground channels. Geologists call this kind of landscape karst, and the Big Bend is full of it.

shots.photo: File:Big Bend Scenic Byway - Leon Sinks Geological Site - NARA - 7717294.jpg
File:Natural Bridge Battlefield Historic State Park Pano.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Natural Bridge, on the St. Marks River

stat.label: Ground dissolved into caves, sinkholes and underground channels

shots.photo: File:St Marks River at Newport, Florida.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The St. Marks River at Newport

paragraphs.text: The clearest proof is the springs. Wakulla Springs, south of Tallahassee, pours out about six hundred and twenty-three cubic feet of water every second on average, roughly four hundred million gallons a day, according to the Northwest Florida Water Management District. Its vent opens about a hundred and eighty feet below the surface into a huge network of flooded caves. And it's not unique. Florida has thirty-one springs that big.

stat.label: Average flow of Wakulla Springs
Depth of the spring's vent below the surface
First-magnitude springs in Florida

paragraphs.text: Some rivers here don't even stay on the surface. The Aucilla River, which reaches the Gulf in the middle of the Big Bend, disappears underground and comes back up again around thirty times along its lower course, according to a state water management plan, before it rises for the last time and runs out into the marsh.

stat.label: The Aucilla goes underground and rises again

paragraphs.text: Look at where those rivers end up. There is no delta, no wide bay to shelter a harbour, no deep river mouth. The rivers fray out into dozens of small creeks and islands of marsh grass, and the shallow sea beyond them goes on for miles. Low land, soft wet ground with holes in it, and a sea you can't bring a ship across.

shots.on_screen_text: Where the rivers meet the Gulf
Marsh islands at the Aucilla mouth

paragraphs.text: So it's not surprising that some of the first big decisions made about this coast were not about building on it. In 1931, an executive order created what is now the St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge, as winter habitat for migratory birds. Today it covers more than eighty-six thousand acres and about forty-three miles of this coast. But seventy years before that refuge, people did try to build a city here. And for a while, it worked.

stat.label: Executive Order 5740 creates the St. Marks refuge

shots.photo: File:A scenic view of white lighthouse.jpg

stat.label: St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge

paragraphs.text: Out at the end of a chain of small islands lies Cedar Key. In the middle of the nineteenth century, this was the spot chosen to connect the Gulf to the rest of the country. Federal surveyors charted its waters in detail in 1852, and in 1861, according to historians of the line, the first train arrived from Fernandina on the Atlantic coast. Cedar Key became the Gulf end of Florida's first railroad across the peninsula.

shots.photo: File:Birds eye view of Florida and part of Georgia and Alabama LOC 99447266.jpg
File:1852 U.S. Coast Survey Map of Cedar Key, Florida - Geographicus - CedarKey-uscs-1852.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: U.S. Coast Survey chart of Cedar Key, 1852

shots.photo: File:Florida Railroad, from Cedar Key Extension to Tampa Bay - NARA - 102256504.jpg

paragraphs.text: The town set out to become a port. According to the town's own history, pencil companies, including Eberhard Faber and the Eagle Pencil Company, built mills on the islands to cut the local red cedar into pencil slats and ship them north. Here is Cedar Key in 1884, drawn from above as a bird's-eye view: wharves, warehouses, a railroad running out over the water.

shots.on_screen_text: Cedar Key from the air (U.S. survey photograph)

stat.label: Faber and Eagle Pencil mills

shots.photo: File:Indian mound, Cedar Key, Fla, from Robert N. Dennis collection of stereoscopic views.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Cedar Key in an old stereoscopic view
Atsena Otie, site of the first town

shots.photo: File:Bird's eye view of Cedar-Key, Fla., Levy Co. LOC 77690244.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Cedar Key in 1884, a bird's-eye view

shots.photo: File:Sanborn Fire Insurance Map from Cedar Key, Levy County, Florida, 1909, Plate 0001.jpg

paragraphs.text: But that same year, the town's future was being decided somewhere else. In 1883, the businessman Henry Plant bought control of the South Florida Railroad and pushed it all the way to Tampa Bay, with full service from 1884, according to the University of Florida's libraries. Tampa had what Cedar Key never really had: a big, sheltered bay. Historians of the town say much of Cedar Key's shipping followed Plant's tracks south. Census counts on record show Tampa growing from seven hundred and twenty people in 1880 to more than five thousand five hundred in 1890.

stat.label: Henry Plant takes over the South Florida Railroad

shots.on_screen_text: Plant's Tampa Bay Hotel (now a museum)

paragraphs.text: Then came the night that finished the boom. On the twenty-ninth of September 1896, a hurricane came ashore near Cedar Key with winds of around a hundred and twenty-five miles an hour. According to the National Weather Service, it pushed the water ten and a half feet above sea level at Cedar Key and around twelve and a half feet at nearby Yankeetown. About a hundred people died, most of them drowned by the surge.

stat.label: Winds at landfall, 1896
Above sea level at Cedar Key, 1896
Deaths, mostly from the surge

paragraphs.text: Accounts of the town's history say the storm destroyed the Eagle mill, and that Faber's mill closed within two years, with the cedar forests already cut out. The town rebuilt on a neighbouring island, but it never became a port again. If you like stories where a map explains what history did, subscribing is how you'll find the next one. Because Cedar Key's collapse didn't end the plans for this coast. Over the next century, Florida tried again.

shots.on_screen_text: Cedar Key from the air (U.S. survey photograph)

shots.photo: File:Sanborn Fire Insurance Map from Cedar Key, Levy County, Florida, 1920, Plate 0001.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Cedar Key and Atsena Otie today
Atsena Otie Key, where the old town stood

shots.photo: File:Sanborn Fire Insurance Map from Cedar Key, Levy County, Florida, 1909, Plate 0001.jpg

paragraphs.text: The biggest plan was meant to cut Florida in half. The Cross Florida Barge Canal would link the Atlantic to the Gulf of Mexico, so ships could cross Florida instead of sailing all the way around it. Its western end was to reach the Gulf at the southern edge of the Big Bend.

shots.on_screen_text: The barge canal west of SR 19

paragraphs.text: Work started in the 1930s, as a New Deal project, and stalled after about three years. In 1964 it started again under President Johnson. Parts of it were dug and built. Then, in 1971, President Nixon halted construction for good, citing the damage it would do to the environment. By then the canal was twenty-eight percent complete, and around seventy-five million dollars had been spent, according to the Florida Museum at the University of Florida.

stat.label: A New Deal start; stalled after about three years
Work starts again

shots.on_screen_text: The finished cut of the barge canal

stat.label: Construction halted for good

shots.photo: File:Marshall Swamp Trailhead; Cross Florida Greenway-01.jpg

paragraphs.text: You can still see a piece of it from orbit. This is where the finished western section meets the Gulf. Look how far the dredged channel runs out to sea, marked by a line of spoil islands, before the water gets deep enough to matter. The rest of the route never became a canal. Today it's the Marjorie Harris Carr Cross Florida Greenway, more than seventy thousand acres of trails and forest across a hundred and ten miles of Florida.

shots.on_screen_text: The channel and its spoil islands
The Gulf off the canal at low tide

shots.photo: File:Florida I75sb Cross Florida Greenway Overpass.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Cross Florida Greenway crossing I-75

stat.label: Of greenway, more than 70,000 acres

paragraphs.text: The Big Bend's other big bet was paper. Near Perry, the Foley pulp mill turned the pine forests behind the coast into cellulose, the biggest kind of employer a county this small can have. On the eighteenth of September 2023, Georgia-Pacific announced that it would permanently close the Foley mill, with about five hundred and twenty-five jobs lost. University of Florida economists estimated the total effect across the state at up to one thousand eight hundred and seventy-nine jobs.

shots.photo: File:Fenholloway River east of Perry Florida.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Fenholloway River, east of Perry

stat.label: Georgia-Pacific: the Foley mill will close
Jobs at the mill
Potential jobs lost statewide

paragraphs.text: That announcement came about two weeks after Hurricane Idalia had come ashore about twenty miles away. So which was the bigger blow to this coast: the storms, or the jobs leaving? Have a think about that one. Because the storms were only getting started, and when they came, they met the same flat seafloor we started with.

shots.on_screen_text: Clearing downed power lines outside Perry after Idalia

ask.text: Which hit harder: the storms or the jobs leaving?

chapters.title: The Same Shelf, Turned Into a Weapon

paragraphs.text: A storm surge is the rise of the sea caused by a storm itself, mostly by its winds pushing water toward land. NOAA lists what decides how high it climbs: the angle the storm comes in at, its strength, its size, its speed, and the shape of the seafloor. On the Big Bend, the wind has fifteen miles of shallow water to push before it reaches the coast.

document.text: Storm surge is the rise in seawater level caused solely by a storm.

shots.photo: File:Hurricane Idalia Batters the Southeastern United States (MODIS).jpg

arrows.label: Wind pushes water over 15 miles of shallows

paragraphs.text: On the thirtieth of August 2023, Hurricane Idalia came ashore near Keaton Beach as a category three storm, with winds of about a hundred and fifteen miles an hour. The National Hurricane Center ranked it the third-strongest hurricane to affect the Big Bend, behind only the Cedar Key hurricane of 1896 and Hurricane Easy in 1950. The surge flooded land eight to twelve feet deep from Keaton Beach to Steinhatchee, and the Cedar Key gauge read six point eight nine feet above the high-tide line, its record at the time. Idalia caused an estimated three point six billion dollars of damage in the United States.

stat.label: Idalia at landfall (category 3)
Strongest hurricane to hit the Big Bend

shots.on_screen_text: The 1896 hurricane on the weather map

stat.label: Surge flooding, Keaton Beach to Steinhatchee

paragraphs.text: Less than a year later, on the fifth of August 2024, Hurricane Debby made landfall just west of Steinhatchee, a category one storm, with surge flooding of up to six feet. And seven weeks after that came Helene.

shots.photo: File:Steinhatchee River from Fort Steinhatchee Pier.jpg

stat.label: From Debby to Helene

paragraphs.text: Helene had grown fast over the warm Gulf. Six hours before landfall, about eighty nautical miles off the coast, it reached its peak: winds of around a hundred and forty miles an hour. It came ashore about ten nautical miles southwest of Perry, late on the night of the twenty-sixth of September 2024, as a category four hurricane. The Hurricane Center calls it the strongest hurricane to make landfall in the Big Bend since reliable records began around 1900. From just west of Keaton Beach through Steinhatchee, the surge put twelve to sixteen feet of water over the land. South of there, through Horseshoe Beach and down to Cedar Key, eight to twelve feet.

shots.photo: File:Iss072e001649 (Sept 25, 2024) -- Hurricane Helene is pictured from the International Space Station as it orbited 257 above the Gulf of Mexico off the coast of Mississippi.jpg

stat.label: Helene at its peak, 6 hours before landfall
Big Bend landfall since records began around 1900

paragraphs.text: This is Keaton Beach in early September 2024, and this is the same coast after Helene. The marsh behind the houses has turned brown. Further south, at Horseshoe Beach, you can see sand and mud washed across the point. On the ground, the day after landfall, the Air National Guard was clearing the roads through what was left of the houses.

paragraphs.text: Fourteen people died in Helene's storm surge, all of them in Florida. The storm went on to kill at least a hundred and seventy-five people across the southeastern United States. Media reports cited by the Hurricane Center say about a quarter of the homes in Cedar Key were destroyed. Three hurricanes had come ashore on the same short stretch of coast in thirteen months.

stat.label: Deaths in Helene's storm surge, all in Florida
Direct deaths across the United States
Of Cedar Key's homes destroyed (media reports cited by NHC)

paragraphs.text: Remember the tide gauge at Cedar Key? We pulled its monthly highest water levels from NOAA and took the highest reading of each year, a hundred and one years of records going back to 1914. Here they are. For most of the century the yearly peak stays below four feet. A few storms in the 1990s and 2016 push it past five. Then Idalia, at nearly seven. And Helene, at nine point three. The two highest water levels in a hundred and one years came thirteen months apart, in 2023 and 2024.

paragraphs.text: NASA's PACE satellite photographed the Gulf the day after Helene came ashore. Along the Big Bend, the sea had turned pale and milky. The storm's winds and waves had churned sediment up from the seafloor across the shallow coastal water. That day, the shelf that shaped this whole story showed up from space.

shots.photo: File:Hurricane Helene Stirs Up Gulf Coast Waters (153390 - pace 20240928 lrg).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Gulf off the Big Bend, 28 September 2024 (NASA PACE)
The Big Bend after Helene, 27 September 2024 (MODIS)

paragraphs.text: So here are the five reasons. A seafloor too shallow for a port or a beach. Ground made of soft, wet limestone full of holes. A boomtown that lost its trade to Tampa and its mills to a hurricane. Plans like the barge canal and the Foley mill that came and went. And a shelf that lets a big storm pile the sea higher here than almost anywhere.

shots.photo: File:Big Bend Scenic Byway - Leon Sinks Geological Site - NARA - 7717294.jpg
File:1852 U.S. Coast Survey Map of Cedar Key, Florida - Geographicus - CedarKey-uscs-1852.jpg
File:Florida I75sb Cross Florida Greenway Overpass.jpg

paragraphs.text: And yet people stay. Cedar Key grew from six hundred and eighty-five people in 2020 to seven hundred and thirty-six in 2024, by the Census Bureau's estimate. Levy County grew by almost five thousand, Wakulla County, south of Tallahassee, by more than three thousand. Much of the coast is protected now, from the St. Marks refuge to the seagrass preserve offshore, and the same shallow water that kept the ports away holds one of the biggest seagrass meadows in the Gulf.

paragraphs.text: Maybe that's what the Big Bend really is: the part of Florida the sea never let anyone turn into the rest of Florida. So here's the question to leave you with. Should Florida keep the Big Bend mostly empty, or try once more to build on it? Tell me where you'd draw the line.

youtube.title: Why Almost Nobody Lives on Florida's Big Bend Coast
youtube.description: Florida has 23.4 million people and a coastline lined with beach towns, yet the long curve where the peninsula meets the Panhandle is almost empty. We measured the seafloor off the Big Bend and compared it with Pensacola and Miami, then follow the karst ground full of springs and sinking rivers, Cedar Key's railroad boom and its fall, the Cross Florida Barge Canal stopped at 28 percent, the Foley mill closure, and the three hurricanes in thirteen months that sent the Cedar Key tide gauge to its highest level since 1914.
